title: How to become an archaeologist in India: routes and careers
seo_title: How to Become an Archaeologist in India: Courses and Careers
meta_description: How to become an archaeologist in India: the study route, field experience, and careers in the ASI, state departments, museums, universities and heritage work.
keywords: how to become an archaeologist in india
summary: To become an archaeologist in India, take a BA in history or a related subject, then an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology, and gain excavation experience. Careers include the Archaeological Survey of India, state archaeology departments, museums, universities and research institutes, and heritage consultancy. A PhD or NET is needed for teaching.

sections.h2: Step one: get clear on what archaeologists actually do
paras: Archaeology in India is a mix of fieldwork, laboratory study, writing, teaching and, for many, administration and conservation of monuments. The romantic image of constant discovery hides months of recording, report writing and paperwork. Knowing this early helps students choose well.

A good first step is a frank conversation with working archaeologists. Our career sessions on [archaeology after Class 12](archaeology-after-class-12.html) and [careers in archaeology, museums and heritage](careers-in-archaeology-museums-and-heritage.html) are built for students and parents weighing the decision.

The standard route is a BA in history, ancient Indian history or a related subject, followed by an MA in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. The MA is the core professional qualification. Some go on to the two-year Postgraduate Diploma in Archaeology at the ASI's Institute of Archaeology in Greater Noida, which gives practical training closely tied to ASI work.

For university teaching, you need UGC-NET (or a state eligibility test) and increasingly a PhD. For research posts, a PhD is generally expected. Our guide to [archaeology courses in India](archaeology-courses-in-india.html) sets out the institutions and programmes in detail.

sections.h2: Step three: field experience and practical skills
paras: Degrees alone rarely make an archaeologist. Directors look for students who have spent seasons on excavations and can be trusted to keep good records. Join your department's excavations, volunteer on other projects where possible, and attend field schools.

Practical skills that make a difference include section and plan drawing, site surveying with a total station or GPS, photography, pottery drawing and classification, GIS, and the ability to read at least one historical script. Workshops in [site mapping and measured drawing](site-mapping-measured-drawing.html) and [archaeological documentation](recording-the-past-a-documentation-workshop.html) build exactly these skills.

sections.h2: Career options for archaeologists in India
paras: Archaeologists in India work in government, museums, academia and a growing private and non-profit heritage sector.
list: Archaeological Survey of India: posts such as Assistant Archaeologist and Deputy Superintending Archaeologist; see below for how recruitment works.
State departments of archaeology and museums: each state has its own department, recruiting through the state public service commission or departmental processes.
Museums: curators, documentation officers and education officers in national, state, university and private museums.
Universities and research institutes: teaching and research posts, usually requiring NET and a PhD.
Heritage consultancy and cultural resource management: impact assessments for infrastructure projects, conservation planning, documentation and site management.
Heritage education, publishing and tourism: walks, lectures, school programmes, writing and media.

sections.h2: Getting into the Archaeological Survey of India
paras: Many students aim for the ASI. Recruitment to several of its posts, including Assistant Archaeologist and Deputy Superintending Archaeologist, has typically been carried out by the Union Public Service Commission through its recruitment-by-selection notices, which advertise individual posts with specified qualifications, rather than through the Civil Services Examination. Vacancies are irregular, and some other posts are filled through the Staff Selection Commission or on contract.

Because eligibility, age limits and procedures change, the only reliable sources are the current notices on the UPSC, SSC and ASI websites. Read them closely: they usually require a master's degree in archaeology or a related subject, sometimes with the PG Diploma or field experience as desirable qualifications. Our session on [ASI, museums and public heritage careers](asi-museums-public-heritage-careers.html) explains how to read these notices and prepare. The guide to the [Archaeological Survey of India](archaeological-survey-of-india.html) explains how the organisation is structured.

sections.h2: Museums, CRM and academia: building a career outside government
paras: Museum careers usually combine archaeology or art history with museology; the National Museum Institute in New Delhi is one route. Cultural resource management (CRM) is still developing in India compared with countries where developers must fund archaeological assessment, but heritage impact assessments, conservation consultancies and documentation projects increasingly employ archaeologists.

Academic careers depend on a strong PhD, publications and fieldwork. Building a clear research direction early matters. A well-made CV that highlights fieldwork and skills helps in every sector; our [archaeology CV and interview studio](archaeology-cv-interview-studio.html) works on exactly that.

faq.q: What qualification is needed to become an archaeologist in India?
faq.a: The core qualification is a master's degree in archaeology or ancient Indian history, culture and archaeology. Many add the ASI's Postgraduate Diploma in Archaeology, field experience on excavations, and for teaching or research posts, UGC-NET and a PhD. Specific government posts list their own required and desirable qualifications in each notice.

The UPSC has typically recruited for several ASI posts, such as Assistant Archaeologist and Deputy Superintending Archaeologist, through recruitment-by-selection advertisements for individual posts, not through the Civil Services Examination. Vacancies appear irregularly. Always check the current notice on the UPSC website for eligibility and process.

faq.q: Can I become an archaeologist after a science degree?
faq.a: Yes. Many MA programmes in archaeology accept graduates from any discipline, and science graduates are valuable in archaeological science, including dating, archaeobotany, archaeozoology, geoarchaeology, remote sensing and ancient DNA. You may need to catch up on Indian history, but your scientific training is an asset.

faq.q: Is archaeology a good career in India?
faq.a: It can be rewarding for people who enjoy fieldwork, research and heritage, but permanent posts are limited and competition is real. Students who combine a good degree with field experience, practical skills such as drawing, GIS or a script, and flexibility across government, museums and heritage work tend to do best.

faq.q: What does an archaeologist do in the ASI?
faq.a: ASI archaeologists explore and excavate sites, protect and maintain monuments, oversee conservation, manage site museums, document antiquities and handle the legal protection of sites under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act. Much of the work in a circle office is administrative as well as technical.
